A bot plays a part by itself; Add Bot in Profiles makes one. When only bots play, the first bot gets the note sounds, so a bot alone lets you listen to a whole part. YARG never saves a bot's score; the score screen after the song shows it, and Left and Right there move between the players. In Profiles, Rename changes a profile's name, Move Player Up and Move Player Down change the order of the players, and Delete Profile asks you to press {ok} again before it deletes. The Difficulties, Scoring and Stars, and Star Power tutorials go further into how a song is scored.
A chord is several frets played together. Its notes sound together with a quick rake, five short bursts rising from dark to bright. Hold all of its frets and strum once.
A chord: {0} together, with the chord rake.
A click marks each note of your turn.
A dark grey highway with a pattern. It turns blue (the groove) while your multiplier is at its highest, and glows orange while star power runs.
A falling sound means listen. From the next bar line, a few bars of notes play with their normal sounds, in the song's rhythm, over the music. You don't play these.

A few of YARG's own settings matter most when you play by ear. On the General tab, Open Calibrator measures the delay of your speakers or headphones: press a button on each tick you hear, and YARG sets its timing so your hits land where you mean them. Run it with the speakers or headphones you play on. The Sound tab has YARG's volumes; turn the music down if the note sounds are hard to hear over it. No Fail, on the General tab, stops songs from failing while you learn, but scores played with it are not saved.
A fixed hit window, 70 milliseconds either side of each note.

A flam is two pads hit a split second apart, one hand just behind the other: both pads play, the second right after the first. Hit them almost together. A roll is one pad hit quickly: its sound repeats fast, so keep hitting that pad, fast and steady, until it stops. A swell does the same on two pads in turn: their sounds alternate, and you hit the two pads one after the other until it stops. In a roll or swell the exact timing does not matter, only that you keep going. They are on Expert, and on Hard in some songs. The practice has all three.

A flam is two pads hit a split second apart, one hand just behind the other: both pads play, the second right after the first. Hit them almost together. With Listen and Repeat on, a roll or swell plays as its separate fast hits in the pattern; play it back as fast as you can until it ends. A roll is one pad, a swell two pads in turn. They are on Expert, and on Hard in some songs. The practice has all three.
A flam: two pads a split second apart, the second right behind the first. Both pads play.
A ghost note on the Red pad: it plays softly, with a whisper. On a kit, hit it gently. Hit the Red pad.
A guitar plays five-fret parts: guitar, bass, rhythm and five-lane keys.

A hammer-on slides up into its note and a pull-off slides down. Play them by pressing or lifting the fret without strumming, right after a note you hit. A tap starts with two wooden knocks: press the fret with no strum. Taps work even after a miss.
A hammer-on to {0}: the note slides up into place. It comes right after a lower note you hit: keep that fret down and press {0}, with no strum.
A held key keeps sounding. Let go after the Let go chimes play. A glissando is a run along the white keys: it plays as one quick slide. Sweep along the keys while it lasts.

A held note keeps sounding. Keep the fret down until the Let go chimes play, then let go; letting go late does no harm. Letting go too early plays Hold dropped. On a held star power note, the whammy bar adds to the star power bar.
A held note on {0}: its tone lasts, then the Let go chimes play.
A held note: its tone lasts, then the Let go chimes play.
A missed note plays the Miss sound. Hitting a pad with no note is an overhit: a buzz, then the pad you hit plays quietly. {practice}

A missed note plays the Miss sound. Strumming when there is no note is an overstrum: a buzz, and your streak breaks. Bass plays the same way as guitar, and its multiplier, which multiplies your points, goes up to 6 instead of 4. Lefty Flip in your profile mirrors the frets and their sounds. {practice}
A percussion note, such as a tambourine: a woodblock knock plays just before it. Press your Hit button or tap the microphone.
A percussion note, such as a tambourine: a woodblock knock plays just before it. Press your Hit button.
A percussion note, such as a tambourine: a woodblock knock. Play it back with your Hit button or tap the microphone.
A percussion note, such as a tambourine: a woodblock knock. Play it back with your Hit button.

A profile is one player: a name, a game mode, the part you like to play, a difficulty, the buttons you use and a few settings. YARG needs at least one connected profile before you can play, and each connected profile is one player in the band. Open Profiles from the main menu.
A pull-off to {0}: the note slides down. It comes right after a higher note you hit: with {0} already held, lift the higher fret, with no strum.

A rising sound ends where your turn starts, on the bar line right after the pattern. Play the same notes in the same rhythm, in time with the song. Each note you hit plays the hit sound; a miss plays the miss sound. On guitar, bass and keys a click marks each note's moment.
A roll: one pad's sound repeating fast. Keep hitting that pad, fast and steady, for as long as it sounds; the exact timing does not matter. Rolls and swells are on Expert, and on Hard in some songs.

A run of the same fret or chord plays only its first note, then holds its tone through the run. Keep the fret down and strum on each hit bar sound. To hear every note, turn on Cue Repeated Notes on the YargAccess tab.

A scale: five notes climbing, C, D, E, F, G. Each new pitch has its own Pitch Guide tone: sing each note and hold it until the next. While you sing too far off, a rising sweep means sing higher and a falling sweep means sing lower.

A setlist is a queue of songs played one after another. {hold1} to add a song to it. {colours}. A short tune, the way a song moves: E, D, C, D, then E three times, the last one held.
A soft tick on every beat of the song, stronger on the first beat of each bar, like the beat lines on the highway. Play in time with them.
A star power note on {0}: the sparkle marks it. Hit every note of a star power phrase to fill the star power bar.
A star power note: the sparkle marks it. Hit every note of a star power phrase to fill the star power bar.
A swell: two pads' sounds alternating fast. Hit the two pads one after the other, fast, for as long as it sounds; the exact timing does not matter.

Each lane's sound plays in its own place, from far left for the leftmost lane to far right for the rightmost. If you hear with one ear or play on one speaker, turn on Mono Sound: every cue then plays in the centre, the same in both ears. The lanes still sound different, since their pitch rises from left to right. YARG's own sounds and the song stay as they are.

Each note plays its pitch {lookahead} milliseconds before it reaches the hit bar, the same Look-ahead as guitar. Press the key as the hit bar sound ends. A chord's keys play together; press them together.

Each note plays its sound a short time before it reaches the hit line. That time is the Look-ahead: you have {lookahead} milliseconds on guitar, bass and keys, and {drumlookahead} on drums. On guitar, bass and keys a rising hit bar sound follows and ends at the moment to play. On drums, hit as soon as you hear the sound. Look-ahead and Drums Look-ahead on the YargAccess tab change the time. You play every note of the song.

Each note plays its sound {drumlookahead} milliseconds before you hit it, the Drums Look-ahead. Hit what you hear right away. Pads hit together sound together. A ghost note plays softly with a whisper, and an accent plays loudly with a sharp crack. Every note plays its own pads, repeated ones too, so a beat sounds the way it is played. On Expert that gets busy; learning it by ear is the point.

Each note you hit scores 50 points on guitar, bass, five-lane keys and drums. Pro drums scores 60, and each key on pro keys 120. Each note of a chord scores. Held notes add 25 points a beat. On vocals each phrase scores by difficulty, and a percussion note scores 100. A missed note scores nothing.

Each player has a highway: a track that runs from the back of the screen to the front, with one lane for each fret, pad or key. Notes appear far away and travel down their lanes towards you. Across the near end is the hit line, which YARG calls the strike line, and you play a note at the moment it reaches that line. YARG's default rules give you 70 milliseconds either side of that moment. Lines across the highway mark the beats and the bars of the song. The notes written for one part of a song are called its chart.
Each profile has a game mode: the kind of controller it plays. The game mode decides which parts of a song the profile can play.

Each profile has its own settings: open Profile Settings on the Profiles toolbar of a connected profile. Lefty Flip mirrors the lanes for left-handed players, and the note sounds move with them. Engine Preset sets the hit rules: Default has a 70 millisecond window either side of each note; Casual keeps that window but forgives extra fret presses and early hammer-ons; Precision narrows the window in fast passages, down to 20 milliseconds; and Solo Taps lets solos be played without strumming. Rock Meter Preset sets how quickly you fail: Casual, Easy, Normal, Hard or Unfair. Input Calibration corrects this profile's timing in milliseconds.

Five-fret guitar: a guitar controller with five coloured frets and a strum bar, for guitar, bass, rhythm guitar, co-op guitar and five-lane keys. Four-lane drums: four pads and a kick pedal, and pro drums adds three cymbals. Five-lane drums: three pads, two cymbals and a kick. Pro keys: a 25-key piano keyboard, usually a MIDI keyboard. Four steps get you to your first song. First, get some songs. Second, set up a profile for your keyboard, controller or guitar. Third, learn what happens in a song and which play style you want. Last, choose Quickplay on the main menu, pick a song, then your part and difficulty, and the song starts. The pages that follow take these steps in order.

Four-lane drums have a kick pedal and four pads: Red, Yellow, Blue and Green, from left to right. Each pad plays a note of the song's scale in its place, rising from left to right. The kick is a low note in the centre.

Guitar, bass, rhythm, co-op guitar and five-lane keys use five frets: Green, Red, Yellow, Blue and Orange, from left to right. Each fret has its own sound and its own place: Green is far left and lowest, Orange is far right and highest. Hold a fret and strum to play a note. {starpowerkey}

History has two tabs: History, and Import. {historytabs} The Import tab lists replay files that came from somewhere else: a replay you saved in the middle of a song with Save Replay in the pause menu, or a replay file someone sent you. On the Import tab, moving up past the first entry reaches Import Replay, which opens a file browser to add a replay file. In the file browser, Backspace goes to the folder above and Escape cancels; when saving, Save here uses the file name shown, and File name lets you type another. A replay from someone else plays only if you have the same song and chart.

History on the main menu lists every song you have finished, newest first, in groups: Today, Yesterday, This Week, This Month, Last Three Months, This Year and More Than A Year. Each entry reads the song, artist, stars, part, percent, score, hits and misses, the play style, the speed if it was not 100 percent, any bots, and the date and time. With several players it reads the band score and each player. {side} jump to the previous or next group. {historyhomeend}

Now a whole pattern, as in a song. After the listen sound it plays: {0}. When the your-turn sound ends, play it back in the same rhythm. First it plays right, with the hit sounds.

Now a whole pattern, as in a song: Listen and Repeat works on percussion notes, and you sing the rest of the song as usual. After the listen sound, four knocks play. When the your-turn sound ends, play them back with {0}, in the same rhythm. First they play right, with the hit sounds.

On Beginner every note can be hit with any fret or pad, so you only play in time; pro keys has no Beginner, and on vocals Beginner accepts any pitch. On guitar, Easy usually uses three frets, Medium four, and Hard and Expert all five. Each step up adds notes and faster passages.
On a guitar, tilt it up or press Select to turn star power on.
On drums star power turns on in a fill, which comes only while star power is ready. A slow rise plays through the fill and ends on its last note: hit that note to turn star power on. Listen.

On drums, hit the pad for each lane in time, and the kick pedal for the kick notes. Pro drums also tells toms and cymbals apart. A roll is one pad hit as fast as you can; a swell is two pads in turn. Five-lane keys work like the five frets, with no strum; pro keys uses 25 real piano keys. On vocals you sing into a microphone. YARG scores your pitch and timing, not the words, and any octave counts. The song is split into phrases, and each phrase gets a rating when it ends.

On drums, star power turns on in a fill. Fills appear only while star power is ready: play anything you like, then hit the last note: its rightmost pad, or any of its pads when Activation in Profile Settings is All Notes. Several players can play one song together on one computer, each with their own profile and device. Their scores add up to a band score, and each player's star power raises the score of the others too. YargAccess is made for one person playing and does not support co-op: only player one, the first human in the band, gets note sounds. Songs move at different speeds, counted in beats a minute, from about 60 to over 200. Songs move at different speeds, counted in beats a minute, from about 60 to over 200. Each sound always comes the same time before its note, the {0}. Songs move at different speeds, counted in beats a minute. In a slow song each pitch has time to settle; in a fast one the pitches change quickly and the Pitch Guide tones come close together.

The notes in the bars where a pattern plays are taken out of the chart, so you play about half of the notes, for example 213 of 410 on Sweet Victory, Hard guitar. Fewer notes means fewer points, so your score is lower than a full play of the same song, and it can't be compared with scores played the whole way through. A full combo needs every note of the chart, so full combos are only possible with Play What You Hear. With Listen and Repeat, YARG shows no Full Combo and none is saved with the score.

The rock meter rises while you play well and falls when you miss. If it runs out, the song fails. YARG then offers to restart, or to carry on with No Fail turned on; with No Fail the score is not saved. No Fail then stays on for later songs until you turn it off. No Fail is in Settings, General tab: On stops failing, and No Meter also hides the meter. The Easy and Casual rock meter presets in Profile Settings make failing less likely; Hard and Unfair make it more likely.
The rules for hitting notes: the size of the hit window and how forgiving strums and frets are.

Vocals score one phrase at a time. When a phrase counts as hit, rated Awesome, the hit sound plays. YARG's rating for each phrase is spoken: Awesome, Strong, Good, Okay, Messy or Awful. Vocals: while you sing a note too far off to score, a rising sweep means sing higher and a falling sweep means sing lower. Silence means you are on pitch. Needs a microphone on your profile.

Welcome to YargAccess. Would you like to open the Tutorials? They explain each game mode, the difficulties, scoring, star power and profiles, with a practice for each instrument. You can open them any time from Tutorials on the main menu, below Practice.
Whammy. Bend a held note. On a held star power note it adds to the star power bar.
When notes are far apart the hit bar sound rises to each one; when they are close, it becomes a click on each note.

When the song's key is known, each fret plays a note of the song's scale, so the chart sounds like a tune. An open note, a strum with no fret held, is a low note in the centre. Strum when the hit bar sound ends: it rises from the note's sound to the moment to strum. In fast passages a click marks each hit instead.

When the song's key is known, each fret plays a note of the song's scale, so the chart sounds like a tune. An open note, a strum with no fret held, is a low note in the centre. With Listen and Repeat on, each pattern plays its notes first; then play them back in the same rhythm. The notes you play back have no sound of their own, only the hit or miss sound. A click marks the moment of each note you play back.
When the timer runs out, the most voted choice joins the show and new choices appear. With no votes, the choices just change
When you play it back, hold the fret as long as the tone lasted.
When you play it back, hold the key as long as the tone lasted.
Whether the highway shows a lane for open notes: never, always, or only when the chart has open notes. Visual only.

While a replay plays, nobody is playing, so the buttons control the replay: {replaykeys} The replay menu has Resume, Restart, Settings and Back To Library. Seeking and speed work while paused too. {help}
While star power runs, your multiplier doubles. YargAccess says Star power on, then Star power off when the bar runs out. Miss a note in a phrase and that phrase is lost: a falling slide plays.
While you sing too far from the note to score, a sweep repeats. A rising sweep means sing higher, a falling sweep means sing lower, and silence means you are on pitch.
With Listen and Repeat on it plays first; then play it back as fast for as long.

With Listen and Repeat on, each pattern plays its keys first, at their own pitches; then press the same keys in the same rhythm. A chord's keys play together; press them together. A click marks the moment of each note you play back.

With Listen and Repeat on, each pattern plays its pads first; then hit the same pads in the same rhythm, in time with the song. Pads hit together sound together. A ghost note plays softly with a whisper, and an accent plays loudly with a sharp crack. The hits you play back have no sound of their own, only the hit or miss sound.
With Listen and Repeat on, every note of a pattern plays, repeated notes too, so you hear exactly what to play back.
With Listen and Repeat on, the percussion note comes as a call: after the listen sound the knock plays, and when the your-turn sound ends you play it back.

With Play What You Hear, each note's sound plays a little before you must hit it. Look-ahead sets how long before, on guitar, bass and keys: you have {lookahead} milliseconds. Drums Look-ahead does the same on drums: you have {drumlookahead}. If your hits keep coming late, raise it; if they come early, lower it. 300 milliseconds is recommended for guitar, and 200 for drums, which have no fret to reach.

Within a game mode you can play more than one part: guitar or bass, for example. Instrument on the toolbar picks the part you prefer, with {adjust}. Before each song, the difficulty screen asks for your part and difficulty. The profile remembers the difficulty; the part starts at your Instrument choice each time, when the song has it.
Y is Play A Show, X opens Filters and LB More Options

YARG comes with no songs, and its menus are silent until you have some, because the menu music comes from your songs. The YARG Access launcher gets them for you: its DLC tab has YARG's official setlists, and its Download songs through Chorus tab finds single songs made by players. Songs you already have, such as songs from Clone Hero or ones a friend gave you, go in a song folder that you add in YARG's Settings.

YARG has Beginner, Easy, Medium, Hard and Expert, and on drums Expert+. You choose for each song on the difficulty screen, after picking the song and your instrument. Your profile remembers the difficulty.

YARG looks for songs in the song folders listed in its Settings, on the Songs tab, and in any folder inside them. The folder controls sit above the first setting: from the first setting, move up. First come Add New Folder, Scan Songs, and Errors Found when YARG could not read some songs. Below them, each song folder has three items: its path, Browse, and Remove folder.

YARG only finds new or changed songs when it scans. Choose Scan Songs after adding a folder, after copying songs into one, or after the launcher downloads a song while YARG is open. YARG also scans each time it starts. A long scan says Scanning songs, and at the end you hear how many songs are in the library.

YARG saves a replay of every song you finish: each button you pressed and when. Watching it plays the song again exactly as you played it, with the same note sounds and hit and miss sounds, at the speed you played. {ok} on an entry watches its replay. A replay needs the same chart: if the song was deleted or changed, YARG says the song is unavailable or the replay can't be played.
YARG's colours: Green, Red, Yellow, Blue and Orange frets and notes, purple open notes, white star power notes, grey missed notes.
YARG's own look: notes are flat rectangular bars across their lanes, and the frets at the strike line are flat buttons. Works for every instrument.
YARG's own sound: a missed note broke a streak of ten or more
YARG's own sound: a star power phrase is complete
YARG's own sound: star power has run out
YARG's own sound: star power is activated
YARG's own sound: the bar is half full, star power can be activated
YARG's own sound: your score reached another star
YARG's own view: the camera fairly high behind the highway, tilted down, and the far end of the highway curves gently away.

YARG's pop-ups during a song. All: note streaks, Hot Start and the rest. Important only: Star Power Ready, Full Combo and New High Score, and when star power turns on and runs out; vocals still reads them all, since the phrase ratings are how a singer hears how a phrase went. Off: nothing.

YargAccess makes YARG playable by ear. Menus are spoken, and during a song the notes are played to you as sounds, so you know what to play. This tutorial takes you from the first start to your first song: getting songs, setting up a profile, how a song works, the two play styles and the song library. Each page is read one sentence at a time: {move} go through the sentences again, {ok} goes to the next page, {side} turn pages, and {back} goes back to the list.

YargAccess turns the highway into sound in one of two play styles. Play Style on the YargAccess tab in Settings picks one, and a change starts with the next song. You have {style} on. Listen and Repeat, the default, plays a few bars of the part, then you play those bars back. Play What You Hear plays every note of the chart just before you hit it: harder, and you play the song as charted. In both, beat ticks follow the beat lines: a soft tick on every beat and a stronger one on the first beat of each bar. The other tutorials follow your Play Style, in their pages and in their practice.

{entrykeys} Export saves a copy of the replay as a file you can share or keep. Deleting asks first. It removes the entry and its score from History for good, and moves its replay to the Recycle Bin. On the Import tab, the same key removes an entry from that list and keeps the replay file. A Listen and Repeat replay is saved with a second file ending in .yargaccess: keep it next to the replay, or the replay plays back the whole chart.

{move} move through your profiles; each reads its name, its part and whether it is connected. {tabs} move through the toolbar. Add Profile makes a new profile, ready to connect, and Add Bot makes a bot. The toolbar changes with the profile you are on: a connected profile has more items than one that is not.

{ok} on a connected profile, or Edit Binds on the toolbar, opens the binding editor. Its Overview tab has Quick Bind, which asks you to press each pad or button in turn. Its Binds tab starts with a game mode list: pick the mode whose buttons you want to change. Then come the actions with their buttons. Add New waits for you to press the button you want; pressing {ok} twice on a button removes it.

{ok} on a profile that is not connected connects it, and so does Connect on the toolbar. YARG then lists your devices: choose the keyboard, controller, guitar, drum kit, MIDI keyboard or microphone it uses. Disconnect frees the profile. Add Device and Remove Device change its devices later, and Devices lists them. A new device starts with YARG's default buttons, so you only need the binding editor if you want different ones.

{pause} pauses the song. The pause menu has Resume, Restart, Practice, Save Replay, Settings and Back To Library; Back To Library ends the song without a score. YARG's most important pop-ups, Star Power Ready, Full Combo and New High Score, are spoken; Speech During Songs on the YargAccess tab in Settings can speak all of them, or none. After the song the score screen reads your results.

{playwithreplay} is Play With Replay: you play the song yourself while the replay's players play alongside you, as if they were in the band. Pick your part and difficulty first, as for any song. Only player one has note sounds: you, or the first bot when only bots play along. The replay's players play without them, so you hear the song and your own part. {blue} plays the song yourself, alone, in your Play Style, as from the song library. {yellow} is YARG's own Analyze: it replays the entry and checks it still gives the same score with this version of the game. The result is only written to YARG's log file; nothing is shown or said.

{practicef2} F3 slows the song and F4 speeds it up. F8 restarts the section. F9 turns section announcements on or off. F1 lists these keys. The note sounds keep their Look-ahead in real time, so a slow song stays playable.
